reason: The shared office service is kept: bounded admission, job sharing by content digest and generation, a transient cache, classified failures and an unavailable answer when no engine exists. What changes: the engine is an operator-installed LibreOffice run as one confined child process per job instead of an npm kit loaded into the host, priorities are not built, source and result bytes are files instead of memory, queue waiting is bounded, and the private output store is not built.

The three on-demand tools office_render, office_convert and office_recalculate are kept as one tools component separate from the service. Activation is read from a fold over the session log instead of an in-memory mark, and converted or recalculated files are written to a path the model names through the filesystem operation service instead of being left in a private store for a shell copy.

The exclusive provider slot is kept: one provider, a second registration fails even under the same name, and the slot is held until the provider's resources close. The Go service adds what upstream left to each provider: a provider interface of plain actions, one fixed tool catalogue, the session-to-browser table, isolation and approval per origin.

The exclusive provider slot is kept. The Go service adds a provider interface, one fixed tool catalogue in which the application is always an argument, the profile an external MCP server must meet, application grants, refused targets, a desktop lease and a fixed unavailable message; it contains no provider of its own.

Upstream's service stores no browser state and leaves session isolation to every provider. The Go browser service owns the table from session to browser, opens one browser per session, runs one call at a time per session, bounds the number of browsers and closes each with its session, so isolation is written once and a provider cannot forget it.
The model still cannot switch the browser backend: configuration selects the one provider and no tool argument names a provider, an endpoint or a mode.
justification: Kept on purpose by decision DH-ADR-MEDIA-1: letting a tool argument choose the backend would let the model, or text injected into a page, select attach mode and with it the user's own logged-in browser. The cost the limit had upstream is removed instead: switching is one configuration edit and the model's tool schema does not change.

reason: Upstream lets concurrent sessions and separate processes operate one desktop and tells callers to coordinate. The Go computer-use service takes a desktop lease for the length of a session's turn, held as a kernel file lock in the user's runtime directory, so a second session and a second dsh process of the same user get computer/busy instead of interleaving input. The user and programs that are not dsh still share the desktop, which the bullet did not cover.
The model still cannot switch the computer-use driver: configuration selects the one provider and no tool argument names one.
justification: Kept on purpose by decision DH-ADR-MEDIA-1: the provider decides what software controls the user's desktop, which is an operator decision and never a tool argument. Switching costs one configuration edit and leaves the model's tool schema unchanged.

reason: Upstream never searches for a system LibreOffice because the engine is an npm package it ships. The Go provider discovers an operator-installed LibreOffice (configured path, standard install locations, then PATH), probes its version and reports path and version in every result and in the status. It still downloads nothing, by owner decision DH-ADR-20. Fidelity belongs to the installed LibreOffice and is reported, not owned.

Upstream's deadline starts only when conversion begins, so time in the queue is unbounded. The Go service has two bounds: queueWait ends a wait as office/busy, timeout ends a run as office/timeout, and the tool pipeline's deadline covers their sum.

Upstream locates only the kit installation it resolves next to itself. The Go provider searches the configured path, a fixed list of standard install locations per operating system and PATH, and runs discovery again at most every reprobeInterval so that installing LibreOffice needs no restart. It still installs nothing, by DH-ADR-20.

Upstream stores converted and recalculated files in a private output directory and makes the caller copy them. The Go tools write the result to the path the model names through the filesystem operation service, under the same policy as any write; the private output store, its retention and its per-session release are not built. Rendered images are stored as attachments.

The bullet describes mapping an engine path out of an Electron application archive (the .asar to .asar.unpacked rewrite) for an npm package. It exists only because of the Node package and the Electron desktop build; the Go harness has neither, and its engine is a program found on disk and probed before use.

Upstream's filesystem service creates no binary files, so the model must copy a temporary file with the shell and a deployment without a shell cannot deliver a conversion. In Go office_convert and office_recalculate take a required output path and write it through the filesystem operation service; no temporary file, no shell copy and no retention deadline exist.

Upstream refuses conversion on a remote workspace because a remote shell cannot read the host's output store. In Go the input is read through the session's filesystem provider into a host scratch copy and the result is written back through the same provider, so a remote workspace converts like a local one; the engine always runs on the host.

Upstream's office_render writes no image file. The Go tool takes an optional save_dir and then also writes each PNG as a file through the filesystem operation service, with the same guard as a conversion output.

Upstream's web client shows only the text blocks of a render result. In Go the result carries each page as an image block by attachment reference and the tool's view carries them, and the host renders tool results as HTML from that logged result; the card that shows image blocks is requested from the tool-card UI areas in the deliverable's dependencies.

Upstream runs the native LibreOffice engine inside the host process, outside the sandbox. In Go the engine is one child process per job, started by the one process starter under a policy that allows writes only to the job's scratch directory and the slot's profile and denies the network where the backend can; with no working sandbox it does not run unless the operator opts out.

Upstream loses activation on resume or fork in PTC mode because that mode's request header records only run_code. In Go activation is a fold over the session log (a successful load of a configured Office skill), independent of how tools are presented, and there is no PTC presentation mode (DH-ADR-8); a resumed or forked session has the tools from its first step.

Upstream keeps activation marks in plugin memory, so a hot reload or a disable and re-enable clears them. In Go nothing is kept in memory: the tools component reads the fold office.active from the log each time a step resolves its tools, so reloading the component changes nothing. Code is never hot reloaded.

Upstream fixes a step's tool set before the content of a user-invoked skill is injected, so the tools appear one step late. In Go the user's skill invocation is a logged record committed before the step resolves its tools, and the fold is advanced inside the append, so the very next model request declares the tools. This depends on area A14 logging the skill load before the step view is resolved, stated as a dependency of the deliverable.
Rendering, fonts and pagination still follow LibreOffice and can differ from Microsoft Office; with an operator-installed engine they can also differ between two machines.
justification: Inherent in using LibreOffice as the engine, which owner decision DH-ADR-20 fixes; no design in the harness can make one layout engine reproduce another. The effect is made visible instead: every result and the status name the engine version, missing fonts are reported, and the engine identity is part of the cache generation.

reason: The Go harness exposes office_render with the same name and the upstream arguments input, pages, sheet, range and dpi. Changed: an optional save_dir also writes the PNG files, a spreadsheet without a range is rendered as its printed pages, the result names the engine version, and a worksheet range fails as office/invalid-request until its scenario passes.

The Go harness exposes office_convert with the same name, formats and sheet rule. Changed: a required output path and an optional overwrite flag; the file is written there through the filesystem operation service and the result holds no temporary path.

The Go harness exposes office_recalculate with the same name and the xlsx and ods output formats. Changed: a required output path and an optional overwrite flag, as for office_convert; a LibreOffice version that ignores the recalculate-on-load setting gives office/unsupported-format instead of stale numbers.

Replaced by two Go config structs: office.Config (queue, reader, source-byte, cache, timeout, input, output, archive and font-file limits with upstream's defaults, plus the new queueWait) and the engine's config (path, confinement, reprobeInterval, minVersion). Not carried: maxBackgroundConversions (no priorities), the three output-store fields (no output store), and fontFallbacks and maxLoadedFontBytes, which configure the kit's own font loader.
Replaced by the config struct of the office.tools component with the same five fields and defaults: activationSkills, maxImages, maxImagePixels, maxImageDimension and maxImageBytes.

ctx.browserUse becomes the service key browser.Key with interface browser.Service: Register(provider) as an exclusive effect, Status, and For(session), which returns that session's browser. Registration now carries a provider that implements browser.Provider instead of a bare name.

ctx.computerUse becomes the service key computer.Key with interface computer.Service: Register(provider) as an exclusive effect and Status. Registration carries a provider that implements computer.Provider instead of a bare name.

ctx.officeKit becomes the service key office.Key with interface office.Service: Status, PDF, Convert, Recalculate and Images. The engine is a second key, office.EngineKey, so the engine can change without touching the service's consumers. The two remote methods are not carried: the preview route calls the service in process.

Final verdict after reading the note: keep the exclusive provider slot and browser ownership by one live session; change the central choice of a name-only registry with no common action interface. The note rejects a unified interface because no consumer needs interchangeable methods; outcome DH-O-10 is that consumer, and with the Stagehand AI layer dropped (DH-ADR-24) every backend offers the same plain actions. The Stagehand, worker and private-model parts of the note are dropped by DH-ADR-24; MCP client start-up at agent creation is replaced by opening a browser on the first tool call.

Final verdict after reading the note: keep the exclusive provider slot; change the rest. A harness-owned tool catalogue in which the application is always an argument replaces provider-owned catalogues, because application grants can be enforced only where the harness can read the target. The in-process native provider the note adds is ruled out by DH-ADR-19, leaving the external MCP server as the only route. The session ownership broker the note rejects is adopted as a desktop lease held for one turn.

Final verdict after reading the note: replace. The note keeps the engine in its own repository and consumes it as an exact npm version with packaging and redistribution duties. The Go harness consumes no engine package at all: the engine is the LibreOffice the operator installed, found on disk and run as a child process, so there is nothing to version, package or redistribute; the harness owns only the adapter, the limits and the lifetime, as the note already assigns to it.

Final verdict after reading the note: keep. Admission before source bytes are read, bounds on readers, queue, source bytes and conversions, identity by exact content digest plus engine generation, a bounded transient cache that never bypasses authorisation, and the rule that only the last reader cancels shared work all carry over. Changed: no foreground and background priorities, bytes are spooled to files instead of held in memory, and the wait in the queue has its own bound.

Final verdict after reading the note: keep three host tools behind the shared service, declared only after an Office skill loads, with rendered images stored as attachments and a route without image input refused. Changed three things. The engine runs as a confined child process and not in the host, because the Go design starts it under a profile written for it. Outputs are written through the filesystem operation service instead of a private store plus a shell copy, because that service governs every write in Go. Activation is a fold over the log instead of a WeakSet plus the last request header, the option the note rejected for cost.

Final verdict after reading the proposal: adopt it. The Go office queue has general resource limits only and no priority field, promotion, demotion, eviction of speculative work or background concurrency counter, because no caller submits background work. Priorities can be added when a real prewarming consumer defines what it needs.
